walkthroughs.body_html:
Changing Urban Areas — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Changing Urban Areas brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Changing Urban Areas.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What are Rio's informal settlements called?
options: Slums
Favelas
Bidonvilles
Townships

mcqs.q: Why do informal settlements develop in rapidly growing cities?
options: People choose slums because they prefer not to live in proper housing.
Informal settlements are theme parks built by councils.
Regeneration means demolishing the whole city.
Because migration and natural increase outpace the supply of formal housing, so low-income arrivals build their own homes on marginal land without legal tenure.

mcqs.q: Is the CBD the most densely populated part of a city?
options: No — the Central Business District has the highest land values and daytime crowds, but few residents; residential density usually peaks in the zones around it.
Most city residents live right in the city centre.
The CBD is where cows are kept in cities.
Informal settlements are theme parks built by councils.

mcqs.q: Does urban regeneration benefit all of an area's original residents?
options: Informal settlements are theme parks built by councils.
Improving an area automatically helps everyone who lives there.
Regeneration means demolishing the whole city.
Not always — regeneration brings investment, jobs and better environments, but rising rents and house prices can displace established low-income communities, a process called gentrification.
